etymology: A modern small-group catchphrase popularized in the church-growth and small-group movements of the 1990s-2000s, naming the shared ordinary life of a Christian community — meals, calendars, crises, and celebrations held in common. A soft, contemporary rendering of an old and weighty biblical reality.
biblical_def: The substance behind the phrase is the New Testament grace of koinonia — fellowship, sharing, partnership in the gospel. The first church gave it flesh: 'they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers' (Acts 2:42), and 'continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house' (Acts 2:46). This is genuinely shared life: bearing one another's burdens (Gal. 6:2), confessing faults to one another (James 5:16), exhorting one another daily (Heb. 3:13), and 'not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together' (Heb. 10:25). The Lord designed His people to be a body, not a crowd of strangers: 'whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it' (1 Cor. 12:26). 'Doing life together,' rightly meant, names exactly this — a people knit together in love (Col. 2:2). The reality is precious; only the phrase is soft.
webster_summary: A soft modern phrase for the shared ordinary life of a church; biblically apt as koinonia (Acts 2:42) but over-used and easily reduced to shared calendars without doctrinal spine.
webster_full: DOING LIFE TOGETHER, phrase. The shared ordinary life of a Christian community — meals, burdens, celebrations, and crises held in common.
A modern small-group coinage (1990s-2000s); a softer cousin of the older language of fellowship, communion, and the body.
Apt sense: the New Testament koinonia of Acts 2:42-46 — doctrine, breaking of bread, prayer, and burden-bearing shared in earnest.
Cautioned sense: thinned to mere proximity and busyness — shared schedules without shared confession, sentiment standing in for the body knit by the truth.
scriptures: Acts 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Galatians 6:2
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
Hebrews 10:24-25

And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
1 Corinthians 12:26
And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it.
Acts 2:46
And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,
corruption_summary: Not a corruption so much as a softening: a weighty word (fellowship) thinned into shared calendars and sentiment, so that proximity and busyness can pass for the body knit together by the truth.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is dilution, not subversion. 'Doing life together' rightly names the koinonia of Acts 2:42 — a real and beautiful thing. The honest caution is that a soft phrase can quietly replace a strong reality. Biblical fellowship is first a sharing in the gospel itself: the Philippians' 'fellowship in the gospel from the first day until now' (Phil. 1:5) was partnership in the truth, not merely the company of friends. Where 'doing life together' comes to mean little more than overlapping schedules — the same gym, the same playdates, the same brunch — the word has been emptied of its doctrinal spine, and a club of likeable people is mistaken for the communion of saints.

The second drift is sentiment in the place of the 'one another' commands. Scripture's shared life has hard edges: it confesses sins to one another (James 5:16), it admonishes the unruly (1 Thess. 5:14), it restores the fallen 'in the spirit of meekness' (Gal. 6:1), it exhorts daily 'lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin' (Heb. 3:13). A fellowship that only affirms and never sharpens is not the body Scripture describes; 'iron sharpeneth iron' (Prov. 27:17), and iron leaves marks. To keep only the warm meals and drop the loving correction is to keep the costume of fellowship and lose its substance.

The recovery is to put the spine back in the phrase: shared life anchored in shared truth. Genuine fellowship flows from common confession — 'that ye all speak the same thing... that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment' (1 Cor. 1:10). Recover the doctrine, the breaking of bread, the prayers, and the burden-bearing of Acts 2:42 together, and 'doing life together' becomes what it ought to name: a people 'knit together in love' (Col. 2:2) around Christ and His Word, not merely a calendar held in common.
roots_summary: A soft modern phrase for shared church life; apt as the koinonia of Acts 2:42 but easily thinned to calendars and sentiment. Recover fellowship with doctrinal spine and the hard 'one another' commands.
roots_lines: English: a 1990s-2000s small-group coinage; a softer rendering of fellowship, communion, and the body.
Greek: koinonia (G2842), fellowship, partnership, sharing — Acts 2:42; Phil. 1:5; partnership in the gospel, not mere company.
The hard edges: Gal. 6:2 (burdens), James 5:16 (confession), Heb. 3:13 (daily exhortation) — fellowship that sharpens, not only soothes.
usage: They called it 'doing life together,' but it was only overlapping calendars; biblical fellowship is partnership in the gospel, not shared brunch.
Iron sharpeneth iron, and iron leaves marks — a fellowship that only affirms and never admonishes is not the body Scripture describes.
Recover the doctrine, the breaking of bread, and the burden-bearing of Acts 2:42, and the warm phrase regains its weight.

verdict.label: Neutral
verdict.line: A warm and biblically apt phrase for koinonia; risky only when it thins to shared calendars without the doctrinal spine of real fellowship.

etymology: A prayer idiom, especially common in American evangelical and older revival speech, asking God's protection and providence over a journey. The plural 'mercies' echoes the Authorized Version's frequent plural — 'the multitude of thy tender mercies' (Ps. 51:1) — and names the many small providences a traveler needs.
biblical_def: To pray for safety in travel is thoroughly scriptural; the believer commits his journeys to God as he commits all his ways. 'In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths' (Prov. 3:6); 'The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore' (Ps. 121:8). Ezra 'proclaimed a fast... that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way for us, and for our little ones' (Ezra 8:21) — an Old Testament prayer for traveling mercies in all but the name. Paul longed to come to Rome 'by the will of God' (Rom. 1:10) and was kept through shipwreck and storm by the God who said 'Fear not, Paul' (Acts 27:24). The mercies themselves are real and daily: 'It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed... they are new every morning' (Lam. 3:22-23). 'Traveling mercies,' simply, asks the God of all our ways to keep us on this one.
webster_summary: A harmless and even apt prayer idiom for safe travel; mildly quaint and easily rattled off, but rightly meant it commits the journey to the God who preserves our going out and coming in (Ps. 121:8).
webster_full: TRAVELING MERCIES, noun phrase. The protection and providence of God sought over a journey.
A prayer idiom of American evangelical and revival speech; the plural 'mercies' follows the Authorized Version's usage (Ps. 51:1; Lam. 3:22).
Apt sense: the believer committing his journeys to God, as Ezra sought 'a right way' (Ezra 8:21) and Paul travelled 'by the will of God' (Rom. 1:10).
Cautioned sense: reduced to a parting pleasantry rattled off without faith — a quaint farewell rather than a real petition to the God who keeps the way.
scriptures: Psalm 121:8
The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore.
Proverbs 3:6
In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
Ezra 8:21
Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river of Ahava, that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way for us, and for our little ones, and for all our substance.
Lamentations 3:22-23
It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
Acts 27:24
Saying, Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar: and, lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee.
corruption_summary: No corruption to name — only the gentle danger of a worn idiom: 'traveling mercies' rattled off as a parting pleasantry, the words emptied of the faith that ought to fill them.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; it is a wholesome prayer-idiom, and the only caution is sincerity. 'Traveling mercies' simply asks God to keep a journey, which Scripture everywhere invites — 'commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass' (Ps. 37:5). There is nothing to recover from the world here. The one quiet danger is the danger of all familiar Christian speech: that a real petition hardens into a reflex, a parting word said as automatically as 'goodbye,' so that the lips move toward heaven while the heart stays on the curb. The Lord warned against 'vain repetitions' and lips that 'draw near me with their mouth... but have removed their heart far from me' (Matt. 6:7; Isa. 29:13).

The phrase can also drift toward a vague good-luck wish, as though 'mercies' were an impersonal fortune one hopes attends the road rather than the personal kindness of a personal God. But biblical mercy is never luck; it is the covenant chesed of the LORD, 'new every morning' (Lam. 3:23), given by Him who 'shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in' (Ps. 121:8). To ask for traveling mercies is to ask Someone for something, not to toss a coin into the air. Where the phrase loses that personal address, it loses the very thing that makes it prayer.

The recovery is small and glad: pray it meaningfully. When you ask traveling mercies for a friend, mean the God to whom you ask it — ask Him to direct the path (Prov. 3:6), to give a right way (Ezra 8:21), to bring the traveler safe to his coming in (Ps. 121:8), and to use the journey for His glory and the traveler's good. A worn idiom prayed in earnest is not vain repetition but a true and tender request, and the God of all mercies delights to hear it.
roots_summary: A prayer idiom for safe travel, mildly quaint but rightly meant; biblical mercy is the LORD's personal chesed, new every morning (Lam. 3:22-23), not impersonal luck. Pray it in earnest, not by reflex.
roots_lines: English: an evangelical/revival prayer idiom; the plural 'mercies' follows the Authorized Version (Ps. 51:1; Lam. 3:22).
Hebrew: the LORD's chesed, covenant mercy and lovingkindness — personal kindness, never impersonal fortune.
Biblical pattern: Ezra 8:21 and Ps. 121:8 — the journey committed to the God who preserves the going out and coming in.
usage: She asked traveling mercies for the family on the road, and meant it — a real petition to the God who keeps the going out and coming in.
A worn idiom prayed in earnest is not vain repetition; the danger is only the reflex that moves the lips while the heart stays on the curb.
Mercy is not luck; it is the LORD's lovingkindness, new every morning — ask Someone for it, do not toss it to the wind.

verdict.label: Neutral
verdict.line: A harmless and apt prayer idiom for safe travel; quaint, and worth praying in earnest rather than rattling off by reflex.

etymology: A church-finance idiom for a freewill, over-and-above gift — collected for a guest preacher, a missionary, a family in need, or a special cause — given out of affection rather than obligation. The phrase joins the affection of Christian love to the ancient category of the freewill offering.
biblical_def: A freewill gift of love is squarely biblical; Scripture commends exactly this kind of cheerful, uncompelled generosity. 'Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver' (2 Cor. 9:7). Under the law the freewill offering stood beside the required ones: 'the men, both heart willing... brought a willing offering unto the LORD' (Exod. 35:22). The early church gathered to relieve the saints (Acts 11:29; Rom. 15:26), and Paul taught that 'they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel' (1 Cor. 9:14), commending the Philippians who supplied his need so that fruit might 'abound to your account' (Phil. 4:17). A love offering, rightly meant, is this very thing: a gift purposed in the heart and given gladly, to honor a servant of Christ or to bear a brother's burden. The category is sound and the motive is commended.
webster_summary: A church-finance idiom for a freewill, over-and-above gift given out of affection; basically sound (2 Cor. 9:7), with only a mild caution against using the warm label to obscure ordinary honesty about money.
webster_full: LOVE OFFERING, noun phrase. A freewill, over-and-above gift collected out of affection — for a guest, a missionary, or one in need.
Joins Christian love to the ancient category of the freewill offering (Exod. 35:29).
Apt sense: cheerful, uncompelled giving — 'not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver' (2 Cor. 9:7).
Cautioned sense: the warm label occasionally used to blur plain accountability — an off-the-books collection where honest, transparent stewardship is owed.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 9:7
Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
Exodus 35:29

The children of Israel brought a willing offering unto the LORD, every man and woman, whose heart made them willing to bring for all manner of work, which the LORD had commanded to be made by the hand of Moses.
Philippians 4:18
But I have all, and abound: I am full, having received of Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God.
1 Corinthians 9:14
Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel.
2 Corinthians 8:12
For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.
corruption_summary: Basically no corruption to name — this is a sound and commended practice; only a mild caution that the warm label must not be used to dodge plain honesty and accountability about money.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the practice is good, and the caution is narrow and practical. A love offering is simply the freewill, cheerful giving Scripture praises — 'God loveth a cheerful giver' (2 Cor. 9:7) — whether to honor a visiting preacher, support a missionary, or relieve a family in distress. There is nothing here to recover from the culture; it is one of the gladder corners of church life. The only danger is the danger that attends all money in ministry: that a tender-sounding label can become a cover for loose or self-serving handling of funds.

The watchfulness Scripture commends is over honesty and motive, not over generosity. Paul was scrupulous to handle the saints' gifts 'honestly, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men' (2 Cor. 8:21), and he 'avoid[ed] this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us' (2 Cor. 8:20). A 'love offering' that becomes an unaccounted, undeclared, preacher-enriching collection — the kind the prosperity hucksters have made a trade of — is no longer the freewill gift Scripture commends but a snare, for 'the love of money is the root of all evil' (1 Tim. 6:10). The cure is plain stewardship: count it openly, report it honestly, give it as designated.

The recovery is simply to keep the love offering what it is — love. Give cheerfully and purpose it in the heart (2 Cor. 9:7); receive it gratefully as Paul received the Philippians' gift, 'a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God' (Phil. 4:18); and handle it transparently before God and men. A church that loves its servants will gladly support them, and a church that fears God will do it in the light. So kept, the love offering is no mere idiom but a sweet-smelling sacrifice, and the cheerful giver is one God loves.
roots_summary: A freewill gift of love, squarely biblical and commended (2 Cor. 9:7; Phil. 4:18); the only caution is plain honesty in handling it — counted openly and given as designated, never a cover for loose stewardship.
roots_lines: English: Christian love joined to the ancient freewill offering (Exod. 35:29) — a glad, over-and-above gift.
Greek: the cheerful giver, hilaron doten (2 Cor. 9:7) — giving purposed in the heart, not grudged or compelled.
The safeguard: 2 Cor. 8:20-21, funds handled 'honestly... in the sight of men' — love offering kept in the light.
usage: They received a love offering for the visiting missionary, counted it openly, and sent it on as designated — a sacrifice wellpleasing to God.
God loveth a cheerful giver; the love offering is gladness purposed in the heart, not a sum grudged or compelled.
Keep it love and keep it honest: the warm label is no excuse for loose handling, for the love of money is a root of all evil.

verdict.label: Neutral
verdict.line: A sound and commended freewill gift of love (2 Cor. 9:7); fine, with only a mild caution to handle it honestly and openly.

etymology: A modern devotional phrase for a peak season of spiritual emotion or vivid sense of God's nearness — a retreat high, a conference glow, a powerful answered prayer. The metaphor borrows from the literal mountains of Scripture (Sinai, Carmel, the Mount of Transfiguration) but locates the value in the experience rather than in the God encountered there.
biblical_def: Scripture knows real heights of nearness to God, and does not despise them. Moses came down from Sinai with a shining face (Exod. 34:29); Peter, James, and John saw Christ transfigured, 'and his face did shine as the sun' (Matt. 17:2), and Peter cried, 'Lord, it is good for us to be here' (Matt. 17:4). These were genuine and given by God. But Scripture also fixes the order: the mountain is not the dwelling place. The Father's voice on the holy mount pointed away from the spectacle to the Son's authority — 'This is my beloved Son... hear ye him' (Matt. 17:5) — and the very next command was to descend: 'And when they were come down from the mount' (Matt. 17:9), straight into a valley with a demon-possessed boy and faithless disciples (Matt. 17:14-21). Elijah's triumph on Carmel (1 Kings 18) was followed by collapse under a juniper tree (1 Kings 19:4), where God came not in wind, earthquake, or fire but in 'a still small voice' (1 Kings 19:12). The height is real; but faith is proved in the descent.
webster_summary: An experientialist phrase prizing the spiritual high; Scripture allows the height (the Transfiguration) but commands the descent — 'hear ye him' and 'come down' — for faith is proved in the valley, not the peak.
webster_full: MOUNTAINTOP EXPERIENCE, noun phrase. A peak season of spiritual emotion or vivid sense of God's nearness.
Borrows from Sinai, Carmel, and the Mount of Transfiguration, but locates value in the experience rather than the God encountered.
Legitimate kernel: God does give real heights of nearness (Exod. 34:29; Matt. 17:2) — not to be despised.
Corrupt drift: experientialism — making the emotional peak the measure of faith, so the ordinary valley of obedience feels like failure or absence.
scriptures: Matthew 17:4-5

Then answered Peter, and said unto Jesus, Lord, it is good for us to be here... While he yet spake, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them: and behold a voice out of the cloud, which said, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him.
Matthew 17:9
And as they came down from the mountain, Jesus charged them, saying, Tell the vision to no man, until the Son of man be risen again from the dead.
1 Kings 19:12
And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.
2 Corinthians 5:7
(For we walk by faith, not by sight:)
Luke 9:33

And it came to pass, as they departed from him, Peter said unto Jesus, Master, it is good for us to be here: and let us make three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias: not knowing what he said.
corruption_summary: The phrase prizes the spiritual high as the measure of nearness to God, so that the ordinary valley feels like failure; but the Mount of Transfiguration ends with 'come down,' and we walk by faith, not by sight.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is experientialism — the quiet conviction that the peak emotion is the spiritual reality, so that having God and feeling a rush become the same thing. Peter made the error first: dazzled on the mount, he wanted to build three tabernacles and stay, 'not knowing what he said' (Luke 9:33). His instinct — pitch a tent on the high place and remain in the glow — is exactly the instinct 'mountaintop experience' nurtures. But the Father did not let him build; the cloud overshadowed, the voice redirected attention from the spectacle to the Son's word — 'hear ye him' (Matt. 17:5) — and the order was to descend. The glory was given, but it was given to send them down, not to keep them up.

The danger of prizing the high is that it teaches the soul to read the valley as abandonment. When a believer makes the retreat-high or the conference-glow the standard of God's presence, the long, dry, ordinary days of duty come to feel like distance from God — and so he chases the next experience as a junkie chases a dose, mistaking emotion for grace. But Christ led the three straight off the mountain into a valley of unbelief and a tormented boy (Matt. 17:14-18); Elijah's fire on Carmel was followed by despair under a juniper tree, where God came in 'a still small voice' (1 Kings 19:12), not another fire. The Christian life is mostly valley, and the valley is where faith is forged: 'we walk by faith, not by sight' (2 Cor. 5:7).

The recovery is to receive the heights as gifts without making them the goal. When God gives a season of vivid nearness, give thanks — but do not build a tabernacle on it, and do not measure His love by it. The proof of faith is not the ecstasy on the peak but the obedience in the plain: feeding the hungry, resisting the sin, keeping the vow, loving the difficult brother on the gray Tuesday when no glow attends it. 'Blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed' (John 20:29). The mature saint walks the valley by faith, carries down whatever the mountain gave, and obeys the One whose voice said, 'come down.'
roots_summary: An experientialist prizing of the spiritual high; the Transfiguration gives the height but ends with 'hear ye him' and 'come down.' Faith is forged in the valley of obedience, for we walk by faith, not by sight.
roots_lines: English: a modern devotional phrase locating value in the experience rather than the God met on the mount.
Biblical pattern: Matt. 17:1-9 — glory given, then 'hear ye him' (v. 5) and 'come down' (v. 9) into the valley.
The forge: 2 Cor. 5:7, 'we walk by faith, not by sight'; 1 Kings 19:12, God in 'a still small voice,' not the spectacle.
usage: He chased the next mountaintop experience as a junkie chases a dose, mistaking the rush for the grace; but we walk by faith, not by sight.
Peter wanted to build three tabernacles and stay; the Father said 'hear ye him,' and Christ led them down into a valley of unbelief.
The proof of faith is not the glow on the peak but the obedience in the plain, on the gray Tuesday when no feeling attends it.

verdict.label: Examine
verdict.line: Real heights are given by God, but prized as the measure of faith they breed experientialism; the mount ends with 'come down,' and faith is proved in the valley.

etymology: A small-group and prayer-meeting idiom: a request offered to be prayed over without disclosing its content — 'I have an unspoken' — trusting God to know the matter while the petitioner keeps the particulars private. A modern, tactful way to seek prayer for a sensitive or shameful burden.
biblical_def: There is nothing unbiblical in asking prayer for a matter you do not name aloud, for God needs no briefing: 'your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him' (Matt. 6:8). Some burdens are too tender, too private, or too shameful to publish, and the Lord receives the wordless groan as readily as the spoken plea — 'the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered' (Rom. 8:26). Hannah prayed so that 'she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard' (1 Sam. 1:13), and God answered. So an unspoken request is a real prayer, and discretion about a private grief is no fault; 'a prudent man concealeth knowledge' (Prov. 12:23). Yet Scripture also calls the saints to 'bear ye one another's burdens' (Gal. 6:2) and to 'confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another' (James 5:16) — which requires that, with trusted brethren, some burdens finally be named.
webster_summary: A harmless privacy idiom for prayer over an undisclosed matter; God knows it unspoken (Matt. 6:8), with only a mild note that habitual vagueness can keep us from the burden-bearing that requires naming (Gal. 6:2).
webster_full: UNSPOKEN PRAYER REQUEST, noun phrase. A request offered for prayer without disclosing its content.
A small-group idiom; trusts God to know the matter while the petitioner keeps the particulars private.
Apt sense: God needs no briefing (Matt. 6:8); the Spirit intercedes with 'groanings which cannot be uttered' (Rom. 8:26); Hannah prayed in her heart (1 Sam. 1:13).
Cautioned sense: chronic vagueness can shield the soul from the burden-bearing and mutual confession that sometimes require a burden to be named (Gal. 6:2; James 5:16).
scriptures: Matthew 6:8
Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.
Romans 8:26
Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.
1 Samuel 1:13
Now Hannah, she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard: therefore Eli thought she had been drunken.
Galatians 6:2
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
James 5:16
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.
corruption_summary: No real corruption — only a mild caution: an unspoken request is a true prayer God already knows (Matt. 6:8), but habitual vagueness can quietly shut out the brethren whom God appointed to bear our burdens.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the practice is innocent and the caution is gentle. To ask prayer for an unnamed matter is no fault, for God 'knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him' (Matt. 6:8), and the Spirit Himself carries the groan 'which cannot be uttered' (Rom. 8:26). Many a burden is rightly kept private — a marriage strain, a wayward child, a besetting sin, a grief too raw for the room — and discretion is wisdom, not weakness: 'a prudent man concealeth knowledge' (Prov. 12:23). There is nothing here to rescue from the world.

The only quiet danger is that the 'unspoken' can become a wall where the soul most needs a window. God did appoint the body to bear one another up: 'bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ' (Gal. 6:2), and healing is promised where saints 'confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another' (James 5:16). A burden never named to anyone is a burden never shared with anyone, and the man who keeps every grief perpetually 'unspoken' may, without meaning to, hold the brethren at arm's length and forfeit the very help Christ sends through them. Privacy that protects can also isolate; shame that hides can also fester.

The recovery is simple wisdom about which burdens to name and to whom. Keep before the wider room what prudence keeps private — the unspoken request is honest and sufficient there. But to trusted elders, a faithful spouse, a close brother or sister in Christ, let some burdens finally be spoken, for 'confess your faults one to another' (James 5:16) cannot be obeyed by a soul that names nothing. God knows the unspoken; that is settled. The question is whether you also let His people, in their proper place, help you carry it (Eccl. 4:9-10).
roots_summary: A privacy idiom for prayer over an undisclosed matter; God knows it unspoken (Matt. 6:8) and the Spirit carries the wordless groan (Rom. 8:26). Mild caution: with trusted saints, some burdens should finally be named (James 5:16).
roots_lines: English: a small-group idiom; prayer sought for a matter kept private, trusting God to know it.
Biblical warrant: Matt. 6:8 (the Father already knows); Rom. 8:26 (the Spirit's wordless groan); 1 Sam. 1:13 (Hannah's silent prayer).
The balance: Gal. 6:2 and James 5:16 — burden-bearing and mutual confession sometimes require a burden to be named to trusted brethren.
usage: She offered 'an unspoken,' and God knew it before she asked — the wordless groan is a true prayer the Spirit Himself carries.
Privacy that protects can also isolate; a burden never named to anyone is help never received from anyone.
Keep before the room what prudence keeps private, but let trusted brethren in — 'confess your faults one to another' needs something spoken.

verdict.label: Neutral
verdict.line: A harmless privacy idiom God already understands; risky only when chronic vagueness shuts out the brethren appointed to bear our burdens.

etymology: A control-term popularized by the Shepherding Movement (the 'Discipleship Movement') of the 1970s — chiefly Bob Mumford, Derek Prince, Charles Simpson, Don Basham, and Ern Baxter — teaching that every Christian must be under the personal 'covering' of a human authority, without which he is 'uncovered' and exposed to Satan. The metaphor turns legitimate, accountable oversight into a near-magical protective umbrella owned by a man.
biblical_def: Scripture knows real, God-ordained authority in the church, and the believer is to honor it: 'Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account' (Heb. 13:17); elders are to 'feed the flock of God... taking the oversight thereof' (1 Pet. 5:2). This authority is real, but it is bounded, accountable, and plural — a plurality of elders (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5), shepherds who lead 'not as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock' (1 Pet. 5:3), serving under the one Head, Christ (Col. 1:18), and under the one final authority, Scripture (Acts 17:11). The believer's true 'covering' is Christ Himself, in whom alone he is hid (Col. 3:3) and whose blood, not a man's permission, shelters him. Legitimate oversight watches for souls and gives account to God; it does not own the conscience, for to one's 'own master he standeth or falleth' (Rom. 14:4).
webster_summary: A Shepherding-Movement control term that can mask authoritarianism, making a man's 'covering' a magical umbrella owning the conscience; recover the real, accountable authority of Hebrews 13:17 over against a covering that claims to own the soul.
webster_full: SPIRITUAL COVERING, noun phrase. The teaching that a Christian must be under the personal authority of a human 'coverer' to be protected from Satan.
Source: the Shepherding/Discipleship Movement of the 1970s (Mumford, Prince, Simpson, Basham, Baxter).
Corrupt use: a controlling umbrella — the 'coverer' grants permission for major life decisions; to leave is to become 'uncovered' and exposed.
Legitimate reality it counterfeits: accountable, plural, bounded eldership that watches for souls and gives account to God (Heb. 13:17; 1 Pet. 5:2-3), under Christ and Scripture.
scriptures: Hebrews 13:17

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
1 Peter 5:2-3

Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind; Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
Colossians 3:3
For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God.
Romans 14:4
Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand.
Matthew 23:8-10

But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren. And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven. Neither be ye called masters: for one is your Master, even Christ.
corruption_summary: A Shepherding-Movement term that recasts ordinary oversight as a near-magical umbrella owned by a man, so that the 'coverer' commands the conscience and the one who leaves is branded 'uncovered'; Scripture answers with accountable, bounded eldership under Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the swelling of real oversight into ownership of the soul. In the Shepherding Movement, 'spiritual covering' meant that each disciple submitted his decisions — marriage, money, employment, moves — to a personal 'shepherd,' and to be outside that covering was to be dangerously 'uncovered,' a target for Satan. The metaphor did the heavy lifting: it converted the bounded, accountable authority of Hebrews 13:17 into a personal umbrella that a man holds over you and can withdraw, so that your safety depended not on Christ but on staying under him. The movement's own leaders later publicly repented of the excesses, and rightly — for the teaching had become a tool of control, not care. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the authoritarian 'covering/uncovered' framing is named here to rebut it.

Scripture forbids exactly this concentration of authority over the conscience. The Lord said, 'be not ye called Rabbi... and call no man your father upon the earth... for one is your Master, even Christ' (Matt. 23:8-10) — precisely to prevent a man from standing where Christ alone may stand. Peter charged elders to feed the flock 'not as being lords over God's heritage' (1 Pet. 5:3); Paul reminded the meddler, 'to his own master he standeth or falleth' (Rom. 14:4). A 'covering' that commands where Scripture is silent, that punishes departure as rebellion against God, that fences a soul off from outside counsel and Scripture-testing (Acts 17:11), has left the office of an elder and become the very lordship Peter forbade. The believer's covering is Christ, in whom his life 'is hid... in God' (Col. 3:3); no man owns that shelter.

The recovery is not to despise authority but to restore its true shape. There is real spiritual oversight, and to scorn it is its own rebellion: elders 'watch for your souls' and the flock is to 'obey them that have the rule' and submit (Heb. 13:17). But biblical authority is plural (a council of elders, not a solitary guru), bounded (binding only where Scripture binds), accountable (the elders themselves 'give account' to God and stand under the Word), and servant-hearted (ensamples, not lords). Submit gladly to that — and refuse the counterfeit that calls itself your 'covering' while reaching to own your conscience. Honor the watchman; bow to no man who claims the place of Christ.
roots_summary: A 1970s Shepherding-Movement control term inflating oversight into an umbrella that owns the conscience; recover the real, plural, accountable authority of Heb. 13:17 and 1 Pet. 5:2-3, with Christ alone as the believer's covering.
roots_lines: English: a Shepherding/Discipleship Movement coinage (1970s; Mumford, Prince, Simpson, et al.), largely repented of by its own leaders.
Legitimate authority: Heb. 13:17 and 1 Pet. 5:2-3 — elders who watch for souls, plural, accountable, 'not lords over God's heritage.'
The true covering: Col. 3:3, the believer's life 'hid with Christ in God'; Matt. 23:8-10, one Master, Christ — no man owns the conscience.
usage: They told her she was 'uncovered' for leaving the group, as if a man's umbrella, not Christ's blood, were her shelter; her life is hid with Christ in God.
Real elders watch for souls and give account to God; a 'covering' that commands where Scripture is silent has become the lordship Peter forbade.
Honor the watchman and bow to no guru: authority is plural, bounded, and accountable, never a man standing where only Christ may stand.

verdict.label: Examine
verdict.line: A control term that inflates oversight into ownership of the conscience; recover the accountable authority of Heb. 13:17, but reject a 'covering' that claims Christ's place.

etymology: From Latin intentio, a stretching toward, purpose, aim. A plain and useful English word meaning done on purpose, deliberate. In the evangelical subculture of the 2000s-2010s it swelled into a near-sacred buzzword — 'intentional discipleship,' 'intentional community,' 'living intentionally' — doing much branding and little real work.
biblical_def: The kernel is biblical and good: Scripture commends purposeful, deliberate living over drift and sloth. 'See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil' (Eph. 5:15-16); 'Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee. Ponder the path of thy feet' (Prov. 4:25-26). The wise man 'looketh well to his going' (Prov. 14:15); the builder first 'sitteth not down... and counteth the cost' (Luke 14:28); Daniel 'purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself' (Dan. 1:8). To be deliberate — to plan, to aim, to choose the good on purpose rather than by accident — is simple Christian wisdom. So far the word names a real virtue. The trouble is not the kernel but the inflation: a humble adjective for 'on purpose' has been crowned as if deliberateness were itself a high spiritual attainment.
webster_summary: A plain word for 'on purpose,' with a fine biblical kernel (Eph. 5:15-16), inflated into an evangelical buzzword that dresses ordinary planning as spiritual achievement — doing more branding than work.
webster_full: INTENTIONAL, adjective. Done on purpose; deliberate; aimed.
From Latin intentio, a stretching toward, purpose — a plain and useful word.
Sound kernel: purposeful living over drift — 'redeeming the time' (Eph. 5:16); 'ponder the path of thy feet' (Prov. 4:26).
Corrupt drift: an evangelical buzzword ('intentional community,' 'living intentionally') that dresses ordinary planning as spiritual achievement — branding in place of substance.
scriptures: Ephesians 5:15-16
See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
Proverbs 4:26
Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established.
Luke 14:28
For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?
Daniel 1:8

But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.
James 1:22
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
corruption_summary: A plain adjective for 'deliberate' is inflated into a near-sacred buzzword, so that calling a thing 'intentional' makes ordinary planning feel spiritual — a word doing more branding than work.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is inflation, not falsehood. 'Intentional' simply means 'on purpose,' and being purposeful is a genuine biblical virtue — 'redeeming the time' (Eph. 5:16), pondering the path (Prov. 4:26), counting the cost (Luke 14:28). The trouble began when the evangelical subculture promoted the adjective to a spiritual rank, so that prefixing 'intentional' to any ordinary activity — intentional coffee, intentional friendship, intentional parenting — lent it an air of holy seriousness it had not earned. The word became a halo: to call a thing 'intentional' was to signal depth and devotion, while often describing nothing more than what 'on purpose' already says. It is branding vocabulary, and like all such vocabulary it can substitute the label for the labor.

The subtler danger is that intending feels like doing. 'I'm being really intentional about this' can become a way of crediting oneself for a resolve never carried out — the deliberateness admired, the deed undone. But Scripture weighs the doing, not the intending: 'be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves' (James 1:22); 'not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord... but he that doeth the will of my Father' (Matt. 7:21). Daniel's purposing in his heart (Dan. 1:8) was honored because it issued in a refusal he actually made and a cost he actually paid. A purpose that warms the conscience but never moves the hands is the very self-deception James warns against, dressed in a fashionable word.

The recovery is to keep the kernel and drop the inflation. Be deliberate — genuinely; plan, aim, choose the good on purpose, redeem the time in evil days (Eph. 5:16). But do not mistake the adjective for an attainment, and do not let 'intentional' become a badge worn in place of obedience done. The mark of a purposeful Christian is not that he describes his life as 'intentional' but that his ways are 'established' (Prov. 4:26) in actual, costly, completed obedience. Let the word mean what it has always plainly meant, and let the deeds, not the branding, bear the weight.
roots_summary: From Latin intentio, purpose; a plain word for 'deliberate' with a fine kernel (Eph. 5:15-16), inflated into a buzzword. Recover purposeful living, drop the halo, and weigh the doing over the intending (James 1:22).
roots_lines: Latin: intentio, a stretching toward, purpose, aim — the plain root of 'on purpose.'
Sound kernel: Eph. 5:15-16 and Prov. 4:26 — circumspect, deliberate walking; redeeming the time.
The test: James 1:22, 'doers of the word, and not hearers only' — the deed, not the intention, bears the weight.
usage: He was 'being intentional' about discipleship for a year and discipled no one; Scripture weighs the doing, not the intending.
A plain word for 'on purpose' got a halo, and prefixing 'intentional' began to lend ordinary errands an unearned air of devotion.
Be deliberate in earnest — count the cost, ponder the path — but let the deeds, not the branding, bear the weight.

verdict.label: Examine
verdict.line: A fine kernel (purposeful living) inflated into a buzzword that brands ordinary planning as spirituality; recover the virtue, drop the halo, weigh the doing.

etymology: A term coined and popularized by progressive evangelical Tony Campolo (with Shane Claiborne and the Red Letter Christians movement, mid-2000s), taking its name from the publishing convention of printing Christ's spoken words in red ink. It signals a professed determination to take the recorded words of Jesus 'seriously,' but functions in practice to privilege those words over the rest of inspired Scripture.
biblical_def: All Scripture stands on one authority, because all of it has one ultimate Author. 'All scripture is given by inspiration of God' — God-breathed — 'and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness' (2 Tim. 3:16); 'the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost' (2 Pet. 1:21). The red letters are precious, but they are not more inspired than the black, for the same Spirit gave both, and that Spirit is the Spirit of Christ (1 Pet. 1:11). Indeed Christ is the Author throughout: 'in the beginning was the Word' (John 1:1), 'by him were all things created' (Col. 1:16), and the risen Lord expounded 'in all the scriptures the things concerning himself,' 'beginning at Moses and all the prophets' (Luke 24:27). Jesus Himself held the whole Old Testament as the unbreakable word of God — 'the scripture cannot be broken' (John 10:35) — and received Paul's letters are 'scripture' too (2 Pet. 3:16). To honor Christ is to honor every word He authored, red and black alike.
webster_summary: Campolo's term elevating the recorded words of Jesus over the rest of Scripture; but all Scripture is God-breathed (2 Tim. 3:16), Christ is its Author throughout (Luke 24:27; Col. 1:16), and the red is not more inspired than the black.
webster_full: RED-LETTER CHRISTIAN, noun phrase. One who professes to privilege the recorded words of Jesus (printed in red) over the rest of Scripture.
Coined by progressive evangelical Tony Campolo (with Shane Claiborne; Red Letter Christians, mid-2000s).
Stated aim: to take Jesus' words 'seriously'; functional effect: to relativize the epistles and the Old Testament beneath a curated 'Jesus.'
Rebutted by the unity of inspiration (2 Tim. 3:16; 2 Pet. 1:21) and Christ's authorship of all Scripture (John 1:1; Luke 24:27; John 10:35).
scriptures: 2 Timothy 3:16
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
2 Peter 1:21
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
Luke 24:27
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
John 10:35
If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken;
Colossians 1:16

For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:
corruption_summary: A movement that elevates the red letters over the rest of Scripture, in practice setting a curated 'Jesus' against the epistles and the Old Testament; but all Scripture is God-breathed, and Christ is its Author throughout, red and black alike.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is a canon within the canon, and the smaller canon is then used against the larger. By naming itself for the red letters, the movement implies that Christ's recorded sayings carry an authority the rest of Scripture does not, and so a soft hierarchy is built: the gentle, quotable Jesus of the Sermon on the Mount is set above Paul's hard teaching on sexuality, headship, and judgment, and far above the Old Testament law. In practice 'red-letter' becomes a lever for moving away from the whole counsel of God toward a progressive ethic, with the texts the movement dislikes quietly demoted as 'not the words of Jesus.' But Scripture forbids this sorting: it is all 'given by inspiration of God' (2 Tim. 3:16), every word breathed out by the same Spirit (2 Pet. 1:21). # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the red-letter elevation is named here to rebut it.

The deeper error is a failure to see who the Author is. The red and the black do not have different authors with the black being lesser; Christ is the author of all of it. 'In the beginning was the Word' (John 1:1); 'by him were all things created' (Col. 1:16); the Spirit who moved the prophets was 'the Spirit of Christ which was in them' (1 Pet. 1:11). When the risen Lord taught the Emmaus disciples, He did not hand them red letters; He expounded 'in all the scriptures the things concerning himself,' 'beginning at Moses and all the prophets' (Luke 24:27). Jesus treated the Old Testament as His own unbreakable word — 'the scripture cannot be broken' (John 10:35) — and the apostolic writings are reckoned 'scripture' on the same footing (2 Pet. 3:16). To pit the red against the black is to pit Christ against Himself.

The recovery is the doctrine of plenary inspiration and the lordship of Christ over the whole Bible. We honor the words of Jesus most truly not by isolating them but by receiving them within the one God-breathed Scripture He authored and authorized. The Christ who said 'love your enemies' is the Christ who inspired 'flee fornication' (1 Cor. 6:18) and thundered 'Cry aloud, spare not' (Isa. 58:1); the same Lord, the same Spirit, the same authority. A true follower of Jesus is not a 'red-letter Christian' but a whole-Bible Christian, who lives 'by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God' (Matt. 4:4) — the very rule Jesus Himself laid down.
roots_summary: Campolo's movement privileging the red letters over the rest of Scripture, building a canon within the canon used against the epistles and Old Testament; but all Scripture is God-breathed and Christ is its Author throughout (Luke 24:27).
roots_lines: English: coined by progressive evangelical Tony Campolo (with Shane Claiborne), from the red-ink printing of Christ's words.
Unity of inspiration: 2 Tim. 3:16 and 2 Pet. 1:21 — all Scripture God-breathed, the red no more inspired than the black.
Christ the Author: John 1:1; Col. 1:16; Luke 24:27 — the whole canon is His word, expounded 'beginning at Moses.'
usage: He called himself a 'red-letter Christian' and used the gentle Jesus to mute Paul; but the same Christ authored both, red and black alike.
The risen Lord handed the Emmaus disciples no red letters — He expounded Moses and all the prophets as the things concerning Himself.
A true follower of Jesus is a whole-Bible Christian, living by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God, as Jesus Himself commanded.

verdict.label: Examine
verdict.line: Elevating the red letters over the rest of Scripture builds a canon within the canon; but all Scripture is God-breathed and Christ authored every word.

etymology: An English rendering of the classical Greek eudaimonia (Aristotle's 'living well,' the good life), revived in modern ethics, positive psychology, and a great deal of recent evangelical writing. Good when it names the full, God-centered well-being of the image-bearer; corrupted when it shrinks into this-worldly self-actualization and affirmation cut loose from holiness.
biblical_def: Scripture does have a vision of human well-being — but it is God-centered, holiness-bounded, and oriented to eternity. Christ came 'that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly' (John 10:10), and the abundant life is fellowship with God: 'in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore' (Ps. 16:11). True flourishing is the blessedness of the man whose 'delight is in the law of the LORD'; he 'shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season' (Ps. 1:2-3) — a flourishing rooted in righteousness, not severed from it. Even the welfare of the city is sought under God: 'seek the peace of the city... for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace' (Jer. 29:7). And the whole of it is ordered to a chief end beyond this life: 'to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever.' Man flourishes when he is what he was made to be — God's image-bearer, reconciled, holy, and glad in his Maker — not when he is merely comfortable, affirmed, or self-fulfilled.
webster_summary: A eudaimonia term, good when God-centered (Jer. 29:7; the abundant life of John 10:10), but weaponized into this-worldly self-actualization and affirmation severed from holiness and eternity.
webster_full: HUMAN FLOURISHING, noun phrase. The full well-being or 'living well' of the human being.
An English rendering of Aristotle's eudaimonia, revived in modern ethics and recent evangelical writing.
Sound sense: the God-centered, holiness-rooted blessedness of the image-bearer — the abundant life (John 10:10), fulness of joy in God's presence (Ps. 16:11).
Corrupt drift: shrunk to this-worldly self-actualization, comfort, and affirmation, cut loose from holiness, repentance, and eternity.
scriptures: John 10:10
The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
Jeremiah 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
Psalm 1:2-3

But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night. And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.
Psalm 16:11
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
Matthew 16:26
For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?
corruption_summary: A good idea — the full well-being of the image-bearer — is shrunk into this-worldly self-actualization and affirmation cut loose from holiness, so that 'flourishing' comes to mean comfort and self-fulfillment apart from God.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the horizontal collapse of a vertical idea. Biblical flourishing is the blessedness of a creature rightly related to his Creator — the tree planted by the water because its 'delight is in the law of the LORD' (Ps. 1:2-3), the fulness of joy found 'in thy presence' (Ps. 16:11). Cut the root and keep the foliage, and 'human flourishing' becomes a purely this-worldly project: psychological well-being, self-actualization, the realization of one's 'authentic self,' material and emotional thriving measured with no reference to God or to holiness. In much progressive and therapeutic usage the word is then bent further, so that 'flourishing' requires the affirmation of whatever a person desires to be — including the very sins Scripture names — and to call any desire to repentance is recast as an obstacle to someone's 'flourishing.' # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the affirmation-as-flourishing framing is named here to rebut it.

Once severed from holiness, the term inverts the gospel's own calculus. Christ asked, 'what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?' (Matt. 16:26), and called His followers to deny themselves and take up a cross (Matt. 16:24) — a summons that the self-actualization version of 'flourishing' cannot comprehend, for it counts the cross as the opposite of thriving. But the man who 'will save his life shall lose it' (Matt. 16:25). A 'flourishing' that crowns the unsurrendered self, affirms it in its sins, and seeks its best life now is not the abundant life Christ gives but the thief's counterfeit (John 10:10) — a fullness that is empty, because it has gained the world and forfeited the soul.

The recovery is to restore the God-centered, holiness-rooted, eternity-bound vision the word once carried. Yes, seek the welfare of the city and your neighbor's good (Jer. 29:7); yes, the abundant life is real and glad (John 10:10). But man flourishes only as what he was made to be — God's image-bearer, redeemed by Christ, growing in holiness, and finding his joy in God Himself. The chief end of man, and so his deepest flourishing, is 'to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever.' True flourishing and holiness are not rivals; the tree flourishes because it is planted by the river of God's law (Ps. 1:3). Sever the holiness and you have not freed flourishing; you have killed the tree and kept the leaves.
roots_summary: A eudaimonia term, sound when God-centered (Ps. 1:2-3; John 10:10), corrupted into this-worldly self-actualization and affirmation severed from holiness. Recover the flourishing of the image-bearer rooted in righteousness and oriented to eternity.
roots_lines: Greek: eudaimonia, 'living well,' the good life — Aristotle's term, revived in modern ethics and evangelical writing.
Biblical flourishing: Ps. 1:2-3, the tree by the river whose 'delight is in the law of the LORD'; John 10:10, the abundant life.
The inversion it forgets: Matt. 16:25-26, save your life and lose it; gain the world and lose the soul — flourishing severed from holiness is the thief's counterfeit.
usage: They called repentance an obstacle to her 'flourishing,' but Christ asked what a man profits if he gains the world and loses his soul.
Cut the root and keep the leaves, and 'human flourishing' shrinks to self-actualization — comfort crowned, holiness forgotten.
The tree flourishes because it is planted by the river of God's law; sever the holiness and you have killed the tree, not freed it.

verdict.label: Examine
verdict.line: Good when God-centered and holiness-rooted (Ps. 1:2-3), but weaponized into this-worldly self-actualization and affirmation severed from holiness.

etymology: A strategy-phrase of the 'winsome,' third-way evangelicalism of the 1990s-2010s — the program of thoughtfully engaging art, politics, and the academy rather than retreating into a subculture. Built on a sound kernel (salt and light) but, in its later 'winsome-era' form, frequently curdled from engagement into accommodation.
biblical_def: The church is sent into the world, not out of it, and so a kind of cultural engagement is commanded. Christ's people are 'the salt of the earth' and 'the light of the world' — 'let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven' (Matt. 5:13-16). Believers are to live among the lost as those who 'shine as lights in the world' (Phil. 2:15), giving an answer 'to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear' (1 Pet. 3:15). Paul engaged the philosophers on Mars' hill, even quoting their poets, in order to preach Christ and the resurrection to them (Acts 17:22-31). But the same Christ prayed that His own, though 'not of the world,' would be kept from the evil while sent 'into the world' (John 17:15-18); salt that engages the meat preserves it precisely by remaining salt. Engagement, biblically, means going into the culture to season and illumine it — never to dissolve into it.
webster_summary: A winsome-era strategy with a fine kernel (salt and light, Matt. 5:13-16) that often curdled into accommodation; recover engagement that stays distinct — salt that seasons by remaining salt — rather than blending in.
webster_full: CULTURAL ENGAGEMENT, noun phrase. The program of thoughtfully engaging art, politics, and the academy rather than retreating into a subculture.
A strategy-phrase of 1990s-2010s 'winsome,' third-way evangelicalism.
Sound kernel: salt and light sent into the world (Matt. 5:13-16; Phil. 2:15) — the church engaging the lost to season and illumine.
Corrupt drift: 'engagement' curdled into accommodation — seeking the culture's approval until the salt loses its savour and the distinctive is dissolved.
scriptures: Matthew 5:13-14

Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men. Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
Romans 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil. They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world.
1 Peter 3:15
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
James 4:4
Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world is the enemy of God.
corruption_summary: A sound strategy — salt and light sent into the world — frequently curdled in the winsome era from engagement into accommodation, seeking the culture's approval until the salt lost its savour and the distinctive dissolved.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the slide from engaging the culture to being absorbed by it. The kernel is genuinely biblical: Christ sends His people in as salt and light (Matt. 5:13-16), and to flee into an isolated subculture is no faithfulness either. But 'cultural engagement,' especially in its later winsome-era form, too often drifted from a strategy of seasoning the world into a posture of pleasing it. The longing for a continued hearing among elites — in the academy, the arts, the prestige press — quietly reset the goal from convincing the culture to being acceptable to it, and the price of acceptability was the soft-pedaling, then the surrender, of the very truths the culture found offensive: on sexuality, on the exclusivity of Christ, on sin and judgment. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the accommodation drift is named here to rebut it.

Scripture names this drift exactly and forbids it. 'Be not conformed to this world' (Rom. 12:2); 'the friendship of the world is enmity with God' (James 4:4). Christ prayed not that His own be taken out of the world but that they be kept from its evil while sent into it (John 17:15-18) — engagement and distinctness held together, never traded against each other. The salt metaphor carries its own warning: salt preserves meat only by remaining salt; the moment it 'have lost his savour' it is 'good for nothing, but to be cast out' (Matt. 5:13). An 'engagement' that achieves a seat at the table by ceasing to taste of Christ has not engaged the culture; it has been swallowed by it, and has nothing left to offer the very world it courted.

The recovery is engagement that stays distinct. Go in — into the arts, the public square, the university, the neighbor's hard question — with the answer 'always... with meekness and fear' (1 Pet. 3:15), genuinely winsome in manner, genuinely present in the culture. But go in as salt and light, set on a hill and unhidden (Matt. 5:14), keeping the savour that makes the engagement worth anything. The aim is not the culture's applause but the culture's good and God's glory: 'that they may... glorify your Father which is in heaven' (Matt. 5:16). Engage to season and illumine, not to blend in; the salt that dissolves into the dish has lost both its work and its worth.
